BEFORE THE
                         FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


In the Matter of the Application of: ​     ​      )
                                                  )
DeepGreen Cook Inlet ​ ​          ​        ​      )​      Docket No. P-15423-000




                                          COOK INLETKEEPER
                                         MOTION TO INTERVENE


        Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”) Rules of
Practice and Procedure, Cook Inletkeeper (“Inletkeeper”) moves to intervene in the
above-referenced proceeding regarding the DeepGreen Cook Inlet preliminary permit application
for the proposed Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub (“Project”). 18 C.F.R. § 385.214. As explained
below, Inletkeeper has a direct and substantial interest in this proceeding that cannot be adequately
represented by any other party. By this motion, Inletkeeper seeks to ensure that industrial development in
the Cook Inlet watershed is completed to the maximum benefit of local residents, our lands, waters, and
the life they sustain.


                                         CONTACT INFORMATION
​       All filings, orders, and correspondence respecting these proceedings and this intervention should
be sent to:


​       Bridget Maryott
​       Cook Inletkeeper
​       3734 Ben Walters Ln.
​       Homer, AK 99603
​       keeper@inletkeeper.org
​       (907) 235-4068




Motion to Intervene
1 of 6
 I. ​    DESCRIPTION OF INTERVENOR
​       This intervention motion is filed on behalf of Cook Inletkeeper (“Inletkeeper”). Inletkeeper is a
501(c)(3) non-profit organization concerned with the Cook Inlet watershed and the life it sustains.
Inletkeeper advocates for the watershed's health through science, legal action, and grassroots organization.
Inletkeeper focuses on programs that protect endangered species, support water quality, conserve salmon
habitat, and build community resilience in the Cook Inlet watershed. We have thousands of members in
Alaska and across North America who share our desire for a balance between industry and environmental
conservation.
​       Inletkeeper has been working to protect the Cook Inlet watershed and the life it sustains since
1994. In pursuit of this mission, Inletkeeper has been actively involved in securing protections for Cook
Inlet beluga whales and all wildlife in the area. The National Marine Fisheries Service (“NMFS”) listed
the Cook Inlet Belugas as endangered in 2008 in response to a joint legal petition filed by Inletkeeper and
its coalition partners.
​       Inletkeeper and its members will be directly affected by the outcome of these proceedings. The
Project is proposed within the critical year-round habitat of the Cook Inlet beluga whale. The population
is fewer than 400 individuals, and NMFS considers Cook Inlet Beluga whales one of nine marine species
most at risk of extinction in the near future. The project may degrade the beluga’s habitat or harm
individual animals by impeding access to the species’ breeding and feeding grounds, reducing prey, or
causing noise pollution that threatens their survival and recovery.
        The project includes “copper-nickel cooling fins” that may release copper into the watershed as
they are scoured by sand, silt, and currents in Cook Inlet. Copper is a known toxin to salmon and may
negatively affect the local salmon population, which residents of the Cook Inlet watershed depend on for
food, recreation, and employment.
        The project relies on “passive subsea cooling” of its data center pods, which will necessarily
contribute thermal energy to Cook Inlet waters. During diurnal periods of slack tide, no current will carry
heated water away from the pods, creating the potential for a warm water mass that could alter the
behavior of salmon and negatively impact the health of all aquatic species. Inletkeeper’s interests in
preventing any harmful impacts of the Project on the Cook Inlet watershed and the life it sustains are
directly at stake. Granting Inletkeeper’s motion to intervene is in the public interest.


II. ​   THE PROPOSED PROJECT
​       On February 11, 2026, DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV LLC (“DeepGreen”) filed an application with
FERC for a preliminary permit for a proposed underwater data center, the DeepGreen Cook Inlet
Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub. FERC accepted an updated application on September 1, 2026.

Motion to Intervene
2 of 6
 The proposed Project would be located in Upper Cook Inlet near Nikiski. DeepGreen identifies an
approximately 1,400- to 1,650-acre project area centered in the deep-water Cook Inlet thalweg. The
preliminary permit would preserve DeepGreen’s priority to apply for a license while it conducts
environmental, engineering, and interconnection studies; construction of the project would require further
authorizations.
         The proposed Project includes a 100-megawatt tidal-energy generation facility and data center. Its
principal components would include approximately 330 to 350 marine hydrokinetic turbines and 66
subsea “hives” (data center pods) with server racks. The proposal also includes construction of scour
skirts and a 3.5-mile subsea cable to connect the offshore hub to a landing site in the Nikiski Industrial
Corridor.


III. ​   GROUNDS FOR INTERVENTION
​        Inletkeeper has and represents interests that may be directly affected by the outcome of the
proceedings, and Inletkeeper’s participation is also in the public interest. Under FERC’s Rule of Practice
and Procedure 214, a party seeking intervention must state “to the extent known” its “position” and basis
in fact and law for its position. 18 C.F.R. § 385.214(b). The party must also state its “interest” in the
proceeding by demonstrating that it has, or represents, an interest that may be directly affected by the
outcome of the proceedings or that its participation is in the public interest. Id. This motion is timely, as
it is submitted before the deadline for intervention established by FERC in its Notice of Application.
FERC, Notice of Preliminary Permit Application for Filing and Soliciting Comments, Motions to
Intervene, and Competing Applications (Sept. 1, 2026).
​        As described above, Inletkeeper is primarily concerned with ensuring that any development in the
Cook Inlet watershed is subject to full and proper regulatory guidelines, and serves the best interests of
the watershed and the life it sustains. Inletkeeper staff and members live, work, and recreate in the Cook
Inlet watershed. The Inlet provides food, employment, and enrichment, all of which depend on a healthy
and robust ecosystem. Members depend on Inletkeeper to hold industry accountable to abide by all local,
state, and federal regulations, and to ultimately protect the health of our watershed. With the support of
our members and coalition partners, Inletkeeper has been actively involved in securing protections for
Cook Inlet beluga whales and all life that depends on a healthy habitat.
​        Our interest is demonstrated by our work to protect the Cook Inlet Belugas and their habitat. The
National Marine Fisheries Service (“NMFS”) considers the Cook Inlet Beluga a species whose extinction
“is almost certain in the immediate future because of a rapid population decline or habitat destruction,
whose limiting factors and threats are well understood and the needed management actions are known and
have a high probability of success, and is a species that is in conflict with construction or other

Motion to Intervene
3 of 6
 developmental projects or other forms of economic activity.” In its 2016 Recovery Plan for the species,
NMFS identified noise as a threat of high concern, with habitat loss and reduction in prey as threats of
medium concern.1
​       Work conducted during the preliminary permit stage of the proposed Project could harm Cook
Inlet belugas and their habitat. Hydrographic surveys and other on-on-the-water work may involve
repeated vessel trips. It is likely to involve echosounders, sonar or other noisy equipment for bathymetry
or other hydrographic surveying. Activities may also include anchoring, placing, and retrieving
monitoring equipment, and disturbing the seafloor. These activities could disrupt beluga behavior and
interfere with the whales’ ability to communicate, navigate, and find food.
        Granting a preliminary permit would also bring more vessels into Cook Inlet during the survey
stages of the Project, including survey boats, barges, tugboats, and maintenance vessels. That traffic could
compound the potential harms mentioned above, and would increase the risk of vessels striking whales.
​       Beyond the preliminary stages, building and operating the Project would add substantial
underwater noise to Cook Inlet. Salmon and other species of significant cultural, economic and
subsistence importance migrate through the Project area annually. Nearly the entire population of Cook
Inlet Beluga whales migrate through the proposed project area twice annually as well. Marine mammals
rely on sound as a primary sense in the silty waters of the Inlet. Installing and operating hundreds of
turbines and computation equipment underwater could create disorienting noise which has been found to
substantially harm a majority of marine biota,2 disrupt marine mammals’ feeding and communication,3
and displace belugas away from critical habitat. Installing turbines, scour-protection structures, and the
subsea cable could stir up sediment, disturb the seafloor, affect prey, and displace whales from feeding
and other important areas. No filings related to the Project have acknowledged the NMFS acoustic
harassment threshold for continuous noise, nor have they mapped isopleths for this threshold under a full
range of tidal conditions.
        Inletkeeper and its members have significant interests in participating in the FERC proceedings,
granting Inletkeeper’s motion to intervene is in the public interest.




1
 See NOAA Fisheries, Recovery Plan for the Cook Inlet Beluga Whale (Delphinapterus leucas), available at
https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/resource/document/recovery-plan-cook-inlet-beluga-whale-delphinapterus-leucas
2
 See Rami El-Dairi et al., Anthropogenic underwater noise: A review on physiological and molecular responses of
marine biota, available at https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0025326X23014133
3
 See Interior Department, Minerals Management Service report: Behavioral Responses of Gray Whales to Industrial
Noise: Feeding Observations and Predictive Modeling, available at
https://www.govinfo.gov/app/details/GOVPUB-I-8a5ac3c4455d7324781c46c42b4b2186
Motion to Intervene
4 of 6
 IV. ​     STATEMENT OF POSITION
​         Inletkeeper seeks to participate in these proceedings to ensure public resource values, including
conservation of Cook Inlet beluga whales, their habitat, and the health and protection of all species.
Inletkeeper also seeks to participate in these proceedings to ensure that any authorization of the Project
complies with all state and federal environmental laws.
​         Inletkeeper opposes the issuance of a preliminary permit due to concerns about the potential
impacts on Cook Inlet Beluga whales, their habitat, and the health of the watershed. Inletkeeper intends to
protect the public interest and uphold environmental laws, as well as all local, state and federal
regulations. Inletkeeper reserves the right to modify this position as more details about the Project
emerge.




V. ​      CONCLUSION
​         Inletkeeper has a substantial interest in this proceeding and the Project’s potential impacts on the
health of the Cook Inlet watershed. Only through intervention will Inletkeeper be able to represent these
interests and seek to avoid and mitigate impacts to the environment, vital salmon populations, and Cook
Inlet Beluga whales. Our interests are not adequately represented by any other party in the proceeding.
Inletkeeper respectfully requests that FERC grant its motion to intervene in the DeepGreen Cook Inlet
Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub Docket No. P-15423-000.


DATED: October 23, 2026
